62. Room (16), wall E: remains of a fresco of the fourth style.

63. Room (16), wall E: the plinth is black, the middle area has an architectural foreshortening in the center and a white panel with a high red border on the side, present only on the left, as on the right the corresponding space was occupied by a door, later walled up and covered with rough plaster. IV style. 79 N60765
1. Atrium (2): view from S-E that allows you to see the triclinium (5) on the right, behind it the rather large staircase for the upper floor and in the background the oecus (7).
2. Triclinium (5): the floor was made of simple cocciopesto; the walls, now completely washed out, show a rough plaster coating.

3. Room (7): the cocciopesto floor with the carpet consisting of crosses of white tesserae, with the central tile black, and the border consisting of a row of white tesserae placed together at the corner, is partly covered by a modern supporting barbican that leans against a brick pillar placed to reinforce the O wall.
5. Room (7), O wall, S section: red plinth; middle area with yellow panel framed by purple borders with purple medallion at the corner.

4. Room (7), wall W with a lararium niche (?): from the faint traces of colour it is still possible to distinguish the simple scheme of the III style with a bipartite structure, with red plinth and middle area, and white upper area.
6. Cubicle (8): on the S wall you can recognize, on the right section, the closure of the recess for the bed. Only rough plaster remains of the pictorial decoration.
7. Room (11), S wall: the pillar in opus vittata mista, leaning against the E wall, was painted in the III style with a black plinth and a red middle area.

8. Room (11), wall O: already in 1868, when Helbig published his work on the painting of the Vesuvian cities, the details of the painting with Narcissus reflected in the water, placed in the central yellow panel, in the center of the middle area with yellow side panels and narrow black compartments with candelabra, could not be distinguished.
9. Room (11), wall O, central section: the narrow black compartment that separates, in the middle area, the red side panel from the central yellow one, exhibits a metal candelabrum.
10. Room (11), wall O, central section: detail of the painting with Narcissus looking in the mirror, now completely illegible.
11. Room (12), S wall with the pillar covered with red plaster leaning against it: black plinth and middle area with rough plaster. 79 N56399
12. Room (12), wall W, against which a modern barbican is leaning; the plaster is now completely washed away. 79 N56966
1. S-shaped external façade of the entrance: red plinth divided into three panels with carpet edges with two parallel lines.
1. S-shaped external façade of the entrance: red plinth divided into three panels with carpet edges with two parallel lines.

2. Atrium (8): the view from the W allows you to grasp the entire depth of the house, up to the bakery behind it (15). In the brick pillars, superimposed on the tuff impluvium, dating back to the primitive layout of the house, the impost of the connecting platforms between one and the other can be recognized, intended to support an attic rather than a valley.
3. Atrium (8): terracotta cistern mouth, bell tower, with lion masks and dentilled frame, datable to the second century BC, placed on the mouth of lava.

4. Atrium (8): tuff impluvium with moulded edge (type A1), the bottom of which was made of large and regular monolithic slabs. The addition of the pillars transformed the original Tuscan atrium into a tetrastyle one. 79 N56454

5. Cubicle (12): the S wall retains traces of the fourth style decoration, probably carried out before the last phase of renovation of the house, carried out in the last period of Pompeii's life. The white plinth is divided into three panels, separated by narrow compartments with a bird in the center, outlined in red; the middle area was also white and followed the same partition.

6. The bakery (15), seen from N-W, was planted in the viridarium, specially paved with polygonal blocks of basalt, and equipped with circular podiums to place the millstones. The N and E walls in opus incerta, present extensive consolidation interventions in opus vittata. In the background you can see the entrance to the room (16) used as a stable for the millstone animals.
7. Bakery (15): the oven with two overlapping arches, seen from N. The structure in opera vittata is very restored in the upper part.

8. Bakery (15): on the W wall, in the section between the warehouse (19) and the tablinum (14), transformed into the vestibule of the bakery, there is a niche above a cistern mouth, and a basin and a masonry counter are attached to it.
9. Bakery (15): detail of the N-E millstone bearing

1. Bottega (17): the view from the W allows you to embrace the entire room, from the threshold in trachyte blocks, with the groove for the folding door, to the partition that delimits the latrine, to the staircase to the upper floor. The cladding of the partition and that of the back wall is in simple cocciopesto.
2. Bottega (17): detail of the latrine with the masonry balconies at the bottom and the high protruding plinth of cocciopesto.

1. The rear façade, along the Vicolo di Modesto, is preserved for its considerable height. Made of reticulated work, fairly regular, it preserves the holes of the construction scaffolding about 2 m from the ground along a horizontal line. Remains of the red plaster coating are preserved only on the corner in parallelepiped blocks of tuff.
2. Atrium (2): tuff impluvium with moulded edge (type B).

3. Tablinum (8), N wall: on the black plinth, now completely discolored, there was the yellow predella; the red middle area had a painting in the center judged by the excavators, who however do not describe the subject, deserving to be detached, as evidenced by the gap in correspondence with it.

4. Tablinum (8), S wall in opus incerta: traces of the predella between the black plinth and the red middle area from which the central painting was detached can be recognized of the decoration in the III style. The upper area was white.

5. Oecus (10), wall O: almost nothing remains of the III style decoration with black plinth divided into panels separated by narrow compartments and middle area with white panels separated by narrow black compartments.
6. Cubicle (11), wall E: the plinth was geometric with a black background with the panels crossed by crosses; the red middle area.
7. Cubicle (11), wall O: from the plaster preserved on this wall it seems to identify the scheme of the middle area with the red panels separated by very narrow black compartments.

8. Cubicle (11), wall $ with the door to the atrium: it is the only one in which the upper white area is also preserved, which follows, in a rectory, for the III style, a succession of colors, the red middle area and the black geometric plinth.

9. Triclinium (12): one of the long walls, the E wall, retains the structure of the subdivision into antechamber and hall. The latter, recognizable in the N section, had, above the now discolored plinth, the tripartite middle area in panels, with a square (carefully removed in the Bourbon era), in the central one.

10. 'Triclinium (12), wall E: the southern section was the antechamber of the room with a now faded plinth and a middle area with a central green panel, two black side panels separated by a narrow red compartment.

11. Viridarium (13), wall E with arched niche with scarce residues of white plaster; the brick altar not aligned with it, was covered with red stucco, above it was painted a lararium on a white background, known from an engraving by Mazois, with Genius sacrificing near an altar placed on his right, towards which two large snakes crawl from below where bushes were also depicted. At the N end the descending downpipe in terracotta tubules is preserved.
12. Reproduction by Mazois who engraved, shortly after the discovery, in 1810 the subject of the lararium in fig. 11.

13. Triclinium (14), N wall: on the W section of the door, the black plinth retains traces of the design that characterized it; a square with a rosette in the center at the point of intersection of a vertical line and a horizontal line that intersect to divide the square into four; the middle area is illegible.

14. 'Iriclinio (14), N wall, section E of the door: the black plinth has a small picture in a contrasting colour (red?) in the centre, in the centre of a thin vertical line; the traces of the separating band towards the middle area can be distinguished.   79 N56470
15. Triclinium (14), N wall, section W of the door: the faded middle area, crossed by a thin candelabrum, retains traces of a vignette.

16. Triclinium (14), wall E: reproduction of the reconstructive drawing made by F. Morelli (Ornati 1829, fig. 64). The black plinth of the antechamber and the hall has an alternation of panels with geometric elements and crossed tirsi, from which hang musical instruments and a plate with fruit (?); in the frieze there are birds and vases. 17. Triclinium (14); the current state of the wall E in which the subdivision into the antechamber, with the yellow panels, and the room with the painting inside the aedicule between the red panels can be distinguished very well.  79 N56472

18. Triclinium (14), wall E: reproduction of the painting now completely lost and already partly vanished at the end of the last century, with Dido weeping, seated on a throne with her sword unsheathed and scabbard on her knees, a clear reference to her suicidal intentions. In front of her is the personification of Africa, recognizable by the elephant remains that cover her head; around the throne the handmaids participate in the queen's grief, while, in the distance, beyond the colonnaded building, a boat can be seen putting out to sea, naturally that of Aeneas.

19. Triclinium (14), S wall: the deterioration of the colours and the gaps caused by the holes drilled in ancient times, make it difficult to recognise the compositional scheme at the back of the room, with a central aedicule with a painting between the yellow side panels. The black plinth and the predella, also black, are completely discolored.  79 N56467

On the opposite side there is a man covered only in the red chlamys, clutching a spear in his left hand. The painting shows Psyche bound and tortured by three cupids in the presence of Nemesis depicted on the left, a subject of which both an allegorical interpretation, linked to the immortality of the soul, and a more "worldly" one, relating to the torments of love, have been given. ADS 134 (Fot. Pedicini)
2. The picture reproduced in the previous figure (H, 854) is currently in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, inv. 1947.288.

3. In another painting in the same room is represented the moment in which Hippolytus, depicted as a young hunter, learns from a letter given to him by the old nurse, that his stepmother Phaedra, depicted sitting on a throne while witnessing the scene, is in love with him, and withdraws horrified at the news.

4. The painting reproduced in the plate of the previous figure (H, 1246) is in the British Museum, from the collection of William Temple, English ambassador in Naples (cf. House VI 9, 6.7, p. 943, fig. 163).

5. In the center is painted Iphigenia, from whom Calchas cuts a lock of hair, while on the right her father Agamemnon, who has consented to the sacrifice of his daughter to appease Artemis so that the Greeks can reach Troy, sits with his head covered (H, 1305). The panel was mounted upside down, as shown by comparing it with the original at the Museum of Naples.
6. Picture with the sacrifice of Iphigenia. AFSN 89820

1. Atrium (2): the impluvium covered with marble slabs dates back to the imperial age; the brick wall that surrounds it is being restored (1977) and is probably a revival of the 'factory prominence with canaletto above for the cultivation of flowers' described by Fiorelli.  77 N37021

2. Atrium (2), S wall: the old photograph is the only preserved testimony of the decoration of this wall, almost completely destroyed during the Second World War. The center of the wall is occupied by a sort of large canopy pavilion, under which in the center is a large thdlos and on the sides two avant-corps with wooden ceilings. The scenographic framing of the wall seems to be juxtaposed with the more usual scheme of the fourth style, with panels with carpet edges separated by compartments with candelabras. From Fiorelli's description it appears that the painting of the atrium was not finished, but executed on only two walls. If the dating of the wall to the phase of the fourth initial style is correct, we should consider this interruption motivated not by the eruption of 79, but by other causes, which in similar situations (V. Strocka, Ein missverstandenere Terminus des Vierten Stils, in RM 9], 1984, pp. 125-140) have been placed in connection with the earthquake of 62.
3. Atrium (2), S wall, section O: the current state of the decoration reproduced in the previous figure, during the restorations (1977).

4. The drawing by G. Abbate (1844) reproduces the cartoon (H, 172) that gave the house its name; it depicts Neptune in the scheme of the Poseidon Isthmios, the statue of the god made by Lysippus for Corinth, also used for the representation of the same deity in the House of the Dioscuri (VI 9, 6-7; cf. fig. 41 on p. 880). The vignette, according to the news of Avellino (cited in bibl., p.87) was located on the S wall of the atrium, reproduced in the previous figures.
5. Atrium (2), O wall, S section: remains of a fresco of the IV style, with a red panel in the middle area. 777 N36545
6. The drawing by G. Abbate (1844) documents the vignette H, 246, from the section of the wall illustrated in the previous figure, representing the chariot of Artemis pulled by two gazelles.

7. Room (3): cocciopesto floor with ornamentation attributable to the first half of the first century A.D. (III style), formed by a network of diamonds and squares outlined in small white tiles widely spaced apart; in the center of the diamonds are crosses formed by five white tiles. The insertion of the marble tiles in the center is to be considered later.

8. Room (3): the detail of the floor highlights how the coloured marble tiles interrupt the ornamentation of white tiles and are therefore probably to be considered a later addition, probably carried out not too far from the execution of the cocciopesto floor.

9. The table of A. Wing executed 'from life in 1844' reproduces the decoration of the N wall of the room (3) (ctr. fig. 10). The vignettes placed in the side panels, however, do not coincide with the sequence of decorations given by Avellino (cited in bibl., p. 88) and must be reproduced from other panels in the same room. ADS 143 (Fot. Pedicini)

10. Room (3), N wall: the black plinth is decorated with a simple geometric motif, still in the tradition of the III style. In the center of the middle area is a flat aedicule with a yellow background with a painting, the red side panels contain vignettes and are bordered by complex borders of carpet in semicircles. A yellow frieze with lotus flower motif, anINS. 5, 3

11. The painting that was in the centre of the N wall (drawing G. Abbate, 1844) depicts Ariadne giving Theseus the thread that will allow him to get out of the labyrinth (H, 1212). The theme appears in another house, VI 14, 38 (Herrmann Bruckmann 1906, fig. 65), considered by Mau to be an imitation of the III style (cf. Mau W, pp. 418, 427), but the comparison with the analogous subject of the House of Lucretius Fronto (cf. Vol.

12. Room (3), N wall, W and central section: detail of the upper area on a white background, with a situla hanging inside a shrine in the centre, and high edges of grotesques and garlands of naturalistically rendered vines. The edges of the triangle and square carpet are already fully of the fourth style.

13. Vignette with a female figure in flight with a basket on her head (G. Abbate, 1844), which, according to Avellino's description (cited in the bibl., p. 88), was located in the centre of the right panel (E) of wall N.

14. Room (3), wall E, section S: black geometric plinth adorned with stretched garlands; the scheme of the middle area is interrupted by the door, the opening of which occupies part of the central aedicule with a yellow background, which does not have the painting on this wall; red side panel and white top area.

15. According to Avellino's description (cited in the bibl., p. 88) the vignette with cupid on the left comes from the central panel with a yellow background (at the door) of wall E (G. Abbate, 1844). The cupid depicted on the right must therefore also have come from this house, as can be seen from the caption, and it is probably identifiable with the cupid with the club described by Avellino (p. 90) in the same room with figures of female divinities (cf. ha 33).

16. This vignette with a female figure in flight with lyra in her left hand (H, 1933; drawing G. Abbate, 1844) which in A. Ala's panel reproducing the entire N wall (fig. 9) is placed in the right panel, comes instead, according to Avellino's description, from the E wall of the room and was located in the centre of the side panel with a red background.
17. Room (3), wall E, section S: the detail of the upper area highlights the 'naturalistic' rendering of the turned ribbon, adorned with fringes and embroidered motifs.

18. Room (3), S wall, section E. Detail of the upper area on a white background: inside an aedicule surmounted by a grotesque border is a griffin in flight; in the corner is represented half of an aedicule with an acroterial sea monster, which is imagined to continue on the wall in the corner; at the top are a rhytòn and a box with a mask.
19. Room (3), wall S: the decoration is symmetrical to that of wall N (see fig. 10); the central panel is not preserved.

20. In the O section of the S wall we must place, according to Avellino's description (cited in the bibl., p. 88) this vignette (G. Abbate, 1844), representing a female figure in flight with kàlathos (H, 1917), which in the Ala panel reproduced in fig. 9 is instead placed, probably for reasons of symmetry, in the left panel of the N wall,  whose cartoon, however, according to the aforementioned description of Avellino, was lost.

21. Room (3), wall W with niche painted on a white background. Black geometric plinth; middle area with central aedicule with yellow background and red side panels; upper area with a white background.

22. Secondoladescrizione di Avellino (cited in bibl., p. 88), this vignette with an emminile figure in flight with a child in her arms (H, 1949; G. Abbate, 1844) comes from the left (S) section of the O. wall ADS 148 (Fot. Pedicini)
23. Room (3), wall O, central section: painting with Apollo standing on the left, in front of Artemis seated on the right (H, 200). 77 N37019
24. G. Abbate's (1844) reproduction of the painting shown in the previous figure. ADS 141 (Fot. Pedicini)
25. Drawing by G. Abbate (1844) reproducing the vignette with a female figure in flight (H, 1903) which, according to Avellino, comes from the right panel (N) of the O wall.

26. Tablinum (5), wall N. In the center of the red plinth is a compartment with a plant; the middle area has a central architectural foreshortening with a purple background and yellow side panels, which contained medallions that are now completely vanid; the upper area is discolored. The passage to the atrium was marked by a pilaster painted with mirrors, of which a remnant is preserved on the left of the photograph. IV style.

27. Tablinum (5): remains of a fresco on wall E, with a red plinth and a middle area with yellow side panels. According to Avellino (cited in bibl., p. 89) a medallion had been detached from this wall, ''nothing left but the circular vow at the site of the tonic'' (cf. figs. 28-29). In the center of the wall, according to the same description, there was instead the remains of a figure of Apollo, near which were the tripod and a snake. IV style.

28. The drawing by G. Abbate (1844) reproduces two of the medallions that adorned the walls of the tablinum (5) of which the barely legible remains are preserved in situ: on the left is depicted Aphrodite with a cupid (H, pp. 76, 278-290), on the right a couple of Maenads and Satyrs (H, 511), the latter coming, according to Avellino (cited in bibl.,  p. 89), from the S wall of the room.

29. Also to the decoration of the tablinum (5) belong the two medallions with pairs of old man (Silenus?) and child and female figure and male figure (Abbate, 1844). Avellino (cited in bibl., p. 89) reports that around the medallion with Silenus (?) there was 'a circular cable... which he attributes 'to the intention that was had to detach him to transport him elsewhere'. ADS 140 (Fot. Pedicini)
30. Room (8), S wall: remains of a fresco of the fourth style with a red plinth and a middle area with yellow panels.
31. Room (10), wall N. Remains of a fresco of the fourth style: the plinth is red, the middle area has a central aedicule (?) with a yellow background and red side panels. 77 N36543

32. Of the decoration of the room (10) are preserved, in the nineteenth-century reproductions by G. Abbate (1844) 1 subjects that were in the center of the panels, representing female divinities. In this one Aphrodite is recognizable naked, with a mirror in her left hand (H, 292).
33. The drawing by G. Abbate (1844) depicts the vignette with Ceres standing with a torch in her left hand and ears of corn in her right (H, 177).
34. This vignette, representing Artemis standing with a bow and arrow (H, 237), also refers to the decoration of the room (10).

35. The two vignettes with cupids reproduced in Abbate's panel probably also adorned the room (10): in the same room in which he describes the figures of Ceres, Venus and Artemis, Avellino describes a cupid with a "beautiful vase (of lustration)". ADS 154 (Fot. Pedicini)

36. This vignette with a mask of Silenus surmounted by a cup, reproduced in the drawing by G. Abbate (1844), is probably attributed to the House of Neptune: the caption reads, in fact, as for all those from this house, "in a house behind the House called the House of the Grand Duke Michael". ADS 157 (Fot. Pedicini)

1. The façade on Vicolo di Modesto, in opus incertum with limestone jambs, cubic tuff capitals, monolithic limestone architrave and tuff cornice; the remains of the plaster coating are preserved. In the foreground, the N section of the façade of House VI 5, 5, with large limestone blocks inserted into the masonry.
2. The monolithic limestone entablature, with square recesses for wooden beams, and the frame in tuff blocks, seen from inside the house.

3. Atrium (2): mouth of a lava cistern dating back to the Republican age, walled up on the E side of the impluvium. The pluteus, restored (1977), takes up the one that had been built on the side of the impluvium and which incorporated the columns of the Corinthian atrium.
5. Room (11), S-wall: the panels of the high red plinth are separated by yellow borders and squared by thin white lines.

4. Room (11), wall N: only here are the remains of the painted decoration preserved, whose simple scheme, with a high red plinth divided into panels, surmounted by a white middle and upper area, suggests that this room (whose location and plan would suggest a triclinary use), had changed its function at the time when the decoration was carried out. Pernice describes the floor, in cocciopesto with a border of white tesserae and adorned with the same material that is no longer distinguishable, which he assigns to the second style. 77 N37008
1. Atrium (2); impluvium with tuff slabs with molded edge, dating back to the Republican age.

2. Peristyle (9), S portico, view from N. The back wall is moved by four semi-columns that occupy the space corresponding to the intercolumnium of the S portico. The half-columns, like the columns of the portico, had the lower part covered with red stucco and the upper part covered with white fluted stucco.  77 N36537

3. Peristyle (9), S wall, central section. In the old photograph, in front of the S wall, the three masonry bases (one of which is covered with marble slabs) are preserved, of which there is no trace in the photograph reproduced in the previous figure: on them rested the three marble statuettes, depicting Hercules with the apples of the Hesperides, Dionysus and a Flora (?) (Fiorelli PAH II, p. 334) donated by Ferdinand II to Grand Duke Michele (Schultz 1838, p. 186; Jashemski 1979, p. 123). Not much better in this old photograph is the state of preservation of the ittura, whose subject is very recurrent on the walls of the gardens painted in the fourth style: above the yellow plinth, the semi-columns framed large windows painted in red, through which the view of a garden animated by birds was imagined:  in the center was "a labrum surrounded by peacocks and other birds" (Schultz 1838, p. 185). On the columns, above a low red frieze with marine animals (and still lifes in correspondence with the capitals?) ran another red frieze, with shoots populated by cupids. In an old photograph, a print of which is preserved at the DAIR, another testimony of the decoration of the peristyle is preserved: the drums of the thin columns painted with bipartite scales described by Schultz (Schultz 1838, p. 185), on which a pergola must have rested. DAIR 31. 2704

4. Peristyle (9), S wall, central section; state of conservation (in 1977) of the friezes: the marine animals and cupids that populate the branch can now only be read in negative. On the other hand, the fall in colour allows a glimpse of the horizontal guide lines that were used for the execution of the shoot (cf. the similar procedure in House VI 2, 14, fig. 44). The stucco frames have the usual lotus and palmette motifs, typical of the fourth style.

5. Peristyle (9), S wall, second semi-column from E: the capital is adorned with a stucco frame with lotuses and palmettes made with a mold which, given the circular shape of the support, included only a palmette between two semilotes. The abacus is in bands, also surmounted by a stucco frame.  77 N36542
6. Peristyle (9): column in the S-E corner, with a capital decorated with a stucco frame.  77 N36541

8. Triclinium (12), N wall, with square window overlooking the garden (15) of House VI 5, 4. The wall, painted in the fourth style, has, above a red plinth with panels separated by compartments with plants, a yellow middle area and a faded upper area.

9. Triclinium (12): in the center of the wall reproduced in the previous figure is this painting, which the small canopy has not been able to protect. The subject, a still life with fish (H, 1707), was suited to the triclinium function of the environment.

10. The shape of the medallion is unusual for a mythological subject (here Polyphemus and Galatea, H, 1047 are depicted). The medallion, reproduced in the drawing by G. Abbate (1844), was probably located in the E section of the N wall, where the overall view (see fig. 8) shows a motif of this shape protected by a canopy.

11. On the E wall of the triclinium (12) there must have been this painting, known from Helbig's catalogue (H, 1774), which cites the drawing by G. Abbate reproduced here (1844). Tools and elements related to sacrifice are depicted: the censer, the cup, the bitter, the knife and the head of the ox.
12. Triclinium (12), S wall: above the red plinth, which is very little preserved here, the yellow middle area is marked by architectural views. IV style. 77 N37003
13. Triclinium (12), S wall, section E: the traces of the medallion with Oedipus and the sphinx within an astragal frame.

14. The drawing by G. Abbate of 1844 preserves the iconography of the medallion (H, 1155) whose remains are reproduced in the previous figure: on the left from behind is depicted Oedipus, who raising his right in a gesture of uncertainty turns towards the sphinx, placed on a high base.
15. Triclinium (12), S wall central section: painting with still life with fish (H, 17707).

16. Also from the triclinium (12), according to Helbig's index (p. 467 III), comes this vignette, reproduced in the drawing made by G. Abbate in 1844, which depicts Leda in flight with the swan in her lap (H, 151), on a yellow background. ADS 158 (Fot. Pedicini)

1. Room (6), wall N: it retains a decoration of the fourth style with a symmetrical scheme, with unusual details, which make us regret the poor state of preservation. The plinth alternates red panels with plants with narrow compartments imitating Numidian marble. Above the plinth is a green predella: in the center there is a still life painted, in which it is barely recognizable
1. Atrium(2):marble impluvium dating back to the imperial age, with rounded strip edge.
2. Room (8): the traces of a cocciopesto floor with ornamentation outlined in large white tiles, in which marble tiles were (subsequently?) inserted.  77 N36535

3. Cubicle (13), N wall, W section, with elevated alcove. The old photograph reproduced here, taken in 1929, presents a typical decoration of the fourth style: the narrow stretch of wall corresponding to the alcove is occupied by a single panel, which seems to have a red background like the plinth, bordered by edges of the carpet in triangles (those arranged horizontally) and shoots (those arranged vertically),  which rest on a stylized Cornucopia; in front of the panel is painted a candelabrum, at which, in the plinth, is a narrow compartment, containing plants like the side panels. At the bottom right you can see how the difference in height between the raised alcove and the antechamber, probably dating back to a Republican age, must have been masked with a sort of 'double plinth' with plants.

4. Cubicle (13), wall O: the wall visible in the previous photograph, on the right of the photograph, has almost completely collapsed. The back wall of the alcove is decorated with a bipartite scheme: in the center of the red middle area is a compartment with a candelabra surmounted by the globe, on the side of which are two panels bordered by carpet edges. Viridarium(14), N wall, central section: in a rocky landscape with trees, the scene of the death of Adonis is represented, framed by two red Ionic columns, preceded by the two statuary groups of Chiron and Achilles and closed at the top by an arched cornice. The handsome hunter, visibly wounded in the left leg from which the blood flows, despite the care of the cupids who cleanse and bandage it, abandons himself in the arms of Aphrodite who supports him with her right. The female figure with Phrygian cap, in an attitude of absorbed sadness, has been interpreted as the personification of the Adonis river whose waters were tinged with the blood of the young hunter; however, it constitutes a reference to the oriental origin of the myth, as is the figure of Aphrodite, a constant presence in the three salient moments of the story (departure for the hunt, wounding, vain aid). The latter, which due to the frequent recurrence in replicas of fixed schemes must have derived from well-known archetypes, probably representations in painting in some famous Adonion, were taken up by Roman sculptors as themes of funerary symbolism. The myth itself on the other hand is imbued with the motif of love and death: Adonis is born from Myrrh's incest and more specifically from the bark of the aromatic tree into which the young girl had been mutated; Aphrodite and Persephone fall in love with him, but the goddess of love will only be able to join him when she helps him on his deathbed. During the festivals in his honor, the Adonies held in spring and summer, women offered small gardens specially cultivated in pots so that they would wither early as Adonis early
